A1.justification: Both PDFs describe GLYCANML with the same core benchmark, datasets and tasks. All pages, figures, tables and equations support comparison. Neither supplied PDF contains a separate appendix; both end with references.

before.justification: Tables 3–4 report original experiments evaluating ten glycan encoders and six multi-task learning methods, with means and standard deviations across three seeds.

after.justification: Tables 3–5 report original experiments, including twelve encoders, taxonomy multi-task learning, and newly added joint taxonomy/function training comparisons.

M1.justification: Section 5.4 adds a training variant that jointly optimizes one function prediction task and eight auxiliary taxonomy tasks by summing their losses. This extends the previous taxonomy-only joint objective; the original encoders, prediction pipelines and six taxonomy MTL algorithms are retained.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same eleven tasks and the same SugarBase, GlyConnect and LectinOracle data, with unchanged sample counts and generalization scenarios. All-atom encoders and joint function/taxonomy training operate on existing task coverage.

E2.justification: Tables 2–3 add Graphormer and GraphGPS across all eleven tasks, introducing an all-atom molecular encoder comparison family and expanding the encoder set from ten to twelve. This substantially broadens comparison beyond glycan sequence and monosaccharide-graph models. All original encoders and taxonomy MTL comparators remain.

E3.justification: Accuracy is replaced by Macro-F1 for eight taxonomy tasks and glycosylation prediction. Section 5.2 replaces unweighted mean rank with weighted mean rank, assigning each taxonomy task weight 1/8 and each other task weight 1. Section 5.4 adds joint-training comparisons. Existing splits, training budgets and the stated validation-accuracy selection rule are retained.

E4.justification: New Section 5.4 and Table 5 test whether auxiliary taxonomy supervision improves immunogenicity, glycosylation and interaction prediction, using both shallow CNN and RGCN. This substantially extends the analysis from transfer among taxonomy levels to transfer into function prediction, including a negative result for interactions.

E5.justification: Both versions specify seeds 0, 1 and 2 and report means with standard deviations. V2 applies the same reporting practice to its added experiments. Changes to individual standard-deviation values do not introduce a new uncertainty estimation procedure.

E6.justification: Tables 3–4 replace accuracy results with Macro-F1 results and revise rankings under the changed evaluation; these are not comparable performance gains. Table 3 adds Graphormer/GraphGPS results and changes some retained AUPRC values, including LSTM from 0.862 to 0.912 and Transformer from 0.729 to 0.856. New Table 5 reports higher immunogenicity/glycosylation means but lower interaction correlations with joint training on both backbones.

T1.justification: The mathematical descriptions of glycan representations and the six taxonomy MTL methods are unchanged. No new theoretical assumptions, propositions, proofs or derivations appear; the metric and aggregation revisions concern empirical evaluation.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion extend the contribution to studying taxonomy-assisted function prediction, and the introduction adds benefits for immunogenicity and glycosylation. The central claims about the eleven-task benchmark, multi-relational GNNs and suitable MTL methods remain.

C2.justification: V2 attributes all-atom models' weakness to the larger atom counts of glycans and motivates taxonomy-to-function transfer through evolutionary similarity, while acknowledging its failure to improve interactions. Section 5.3 narrows the difficult-task benefit to RGCN and changes its example from TS to DTP. The lack-of-3D-coverage limitation remains.

D1.justification: Table 2 adds architecture details for Graphormer—eight layers, 768-dimensional embeddings and 28.5M parameters—and GraphGPS—six layers, 512-dimensional embeddings and 17.4M parameters. Existing training, hardware, software and code/data access disclosures are retained.

R1.justification: V2 adds four cited works: the Graphormer and GraphGPS papers, plus carbohydrate NMR prediction and GlycoNMR references supporting future 3D work. These locally extend comparison positioning and future-work context; the related-work discussion and central novelty positioning remain largely unchanged.

P1.justification: V2 makes localized additions to the abstract, introduction, baseline descriptions and conclusion, updates results discussion, and adds Section 5.4. Most prose and the main section organization are retained, without extensive rewriting or restructuring.

P2.justification: V2 adds Table 5, expands Tables 2–3 with an all-atom model group, and gives Table 3 grouped taxonomy columns and explicit metric labels. Other table headings and pagination adjust accordingly. Figures 1–2 and the overall visual format remain unchanged.

improvement.justification: V1's accuracy-based classification evaluation and unweighted ranking could obscure minority-class performance and let eight related taxonomy tasks dominate the overall comparison. V2 addresses these important benchmark weaknesses with Macro-F1 and balanced task-type weighting, while adding all-atom comparisons and evidence about functional transfer, including negative findings. Together these substantially strengthen the benchmark's usefulness. The new explanation attributing all-atom failures to molecule size remains untested.
